--- title: "Lift charts and Lorenz curves" description: "Does the model separate low risks from high risks? Lift charts, double lift charts, Lorenz curves and the Gini index for pure premium." --- **Question answered:** does the model separate low risks from high risks, and is its prediction right for each risk segment? The [deviance page](deviance.qmd) ended with D² values of about 1\.3%: individual claims are mostly chance, so any average over individual errors is small. A pricing model is judged on something else: whether the policies it calls expensive really cost more, *as a group*, than the ones it calls cheap. Grouping averages away the noise. This page covers the standard tools for that: - the **lift chart**: actual against predicted, by decile of the prediction; - the **double lift chart**: two models compared where they disagree; - the **Lorenz curve** and the **Gini index**: one number for how well a model separates risks. ## The lift chart To draw a lift chart (also called a *quantile plot*): 1. sort the test policies by their predicted pure premium, 2. cut them into 10 groups (**deciles**) holding the same total exposure, 3. per decile, compare the exposure-weighted **average prediction** with the **average actual** pure premium. The deciles hold equal *exposure* rather than equal numbers of policies, because pure premium is a rate per policy-year: a decile full of short policies would hold far less information than its policy count suggests. ::: {#cell-fig-lift .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} lift = {m: segment_table(y, {m: p[m]}, w, sort_by=p[m]) for m in models} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2), sharey=True) for ax, m in zip(axes, models): plot_segments(lift[m], [m], ax=ax, xlabel=f"Decile of {m} prediction (1 = lowest)", title=m) axes[1].set_ylabel("") fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Lift charts on the test set: average actual and predicted pure premium per decile of each model's prediction (deciles of equal exposure). Bars are 95% intervals for the actual average.](lift-lorenz_files/figure-html/fig-lift-output-1.png){#fig-lift width=1087 height=451} ::: ::: A good lift chart shows three things: - **Monotonicity.** Actual cost should rise from decile to decile. Both models get there broadly, with a few dips in the middle. - **Spread.** The steeper the actual curve, the better the model separates risks. The ratio of the top to the bottom decile is a common summary (the 'lift' that gives the chart its name). - **Agreement.** The predicted line should run through the actual points. A gap shows the predictions are off for that segment even when the overall average is right: calibration, checked by group. ::: {#tbl-lift .cell tbl-cap='Summaries of the lift charts. Lift is the top decile\'s actual average divided by the bottom decile\'s (or by the overall average).' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({ m: { "actual, decile 1 (EUR)": t.loc[1, "actual"], "actual, decile 10 (EUR)": t.loc[10, "actual"], "lift: decile 10 ÷ decile 1": t.loc[10, "actual"] / t.loc[1, "actual"], "lift: decile 10 ÷ overall": t.loc[10, "actual"] / mean, "predicted ÷ actual, decile 10": t.loc[10, m] / t.loc[10, "actual"], } for m, t in lift.items() }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
GLM GBM
actual, decile 1 (EUR) 73.68 51.89
actual, decile 10 (EUR) 344.87 380.61
lift: decile 10 ÷ decile 1 4.68 7.34
lift: decile 10 ÷ overall 2.36 2.60
predicted ÷ actual, decile 10 1.23 0.98
``` ::: ::: The GBM's top decile costs 7\.3 times its bottom decile, against 4\.7 times for the GLM. Where the models differ most is the top decile: the GLM predicts 23% more than its riskiest policies actually cost, while the GBM is within 2%. The GLM's predictions are too extreme at the top, the regression-to-the-mean pattern the [calibration page](../binary/calibration.qmd) described for probabilities. ::: {.callout-note} ## Read the intervals before reading the dips Each decile holds 12\,871 to 20\,188 policies, but only 312 to 1\,496 of them have a claim, and claim sizes vary enormously. The 95% intervals are wide, so a dip such as the GBM's 4th decile is well within noise. Don't redesign a model to remove a wiggle that the intervals cover. ::: ## The double lift chart Two lift charts side by side are hard to compare: both look good, and their deciles contain different policies. The **double lift chart** compares the two models directly, on the policies where they **disagree**: 1. put both models on the same overall level (here: rescale each so its average on the test set equals the actual average), so a difference in the overall level doesn't look like a difference in segmentation; 2. sort the policies by the ratio GBM ÷ GLM, and cut them into deciles of equal exposure; 3. per decile, compare the actual average with both models' averages. Decile 1 holds the policies the GBM rates much lower than the GLM, decile 10 those it rates much higher. In the middle the models agree. ::: {#a6b140ab .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} rebalanced = {m: p[m] * mean / np.average(p[m], weights=w) for m in models} double = segment_table(y, rebalanced, w, sort_by=rebalanced["GBM"] / rebalanced["GLM"]) ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-double-lift .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} xlabel = "Decile of GBM ÷ GLM (1 = GBM much lower)" fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.2)) plot_segments(double, models, ax=axes[0], xlabel=xlabel, legend_loc="upper center") plot_segments(double, models, ax=axes[1], ratio=True, xlabel=xlabel) fig.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Double lift chart, GBM against GLM. Left: average actual and predicted pure premium per decile of the ratio GBM ÷ GLM. Right: actual ÷ predicted for each model; 1 means the model's average is right for that decile.](lift-lorenz_files/figure-html/fig-double-lift-output-1.png){#fig-double-lift width=1087 height=451} ::: ::: The left panel answers the question 'who is right where they disagree?' In decile 1, the GLM predicts 349 EUR, the GBM 182 EUR, and the actual average is 255 EUR. In decile 10, the GLM predicts 104, the GBM 226, and the actual average is 159. **Neither model wins:** in both tails the truth lies between them. The right panel shows the same comparison as actual ÷ predicted. The better model is the one whose curve stays **flat at 1**. Insurers read this as a loss ratio: if premiums were set by the GLM, actual ÷ GLM is the loss ratio each segment would produce. - **Actual ÷ GLM rises** from 0\.73 to 1\.53. The GBM finds policies the GLM overprices (left) and underprices (right). - **Actual ÷ GBM falls** from 1\.40 to 0\.71. The GLM finds mispricing in the GBM just as well. Each model knows something the other doesn't, and each overreacts where it disagrees with the other. A curve that crosses 1 in the *opposite* direction would mean the model is worse than useless where the two differ: its deviations from the other model point the wrong way. ### What the double lift chart suggests: blend When both models are partly right, a combination usually beats either. A simple blend is the geometric mean of the two predictions (an average on the log scale, which suits multiplicative pricing models): ::: {#79d49983 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} blend = np.sqrt(rebalanced["GLM"] * rebalanced["GBM"]) blend *= mean / np.average(blend, weights=w) ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-double-lift-blend .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} double_blend = segment_table(y, {"Blend": blend, "GBM": rebalanced["GBM"]}, w, sort_by=blend / rebalanced["GBM"]) ax = plot_segments(double_blend, ["Blend", "GBM"], ratio=True, xlabel="Decile of Blend ÷ GBM (1 = Blend much lower)") ax.figure.set_size_inches(6, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Double lift chart, blend against GBM: actual ÷ predicted per decile of the ratio Blend ÷ GBM.](lift-lorenz_files/figure-html/fig-double-lift-blend-output-1.png){#fig-double-lift-blend width=589 height=447} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-blend .cell tbl-cap='Gini index and D² (Tweedie, p = 1.9) of the two models and their blend on the test set.' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} scores = {**{m: p[m] for m in models}, "Blend": blend} pd.DataFrame({ m: {"Gini": gini_index(y, s, w), "D²": deviance_metrics(y, s, p["Null"], w, TWEEDIE_POWER)["D²"]} for m, s in scores.items() }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
GLM GBM Blend
Gini 0.2928 0.2944 0.3078
D² 0.0127 0.0134 0.0147
``` ::: ::: Against the blend, the GBM's actual ÷ predicted swings away from 1 at both ends, while the blend's stays near 1 within the noise: in this pairing, the blend wins. The blend also has the highest Gini and D². Two caveats: the comparison is on the test set the double lift chart was read from, so a blend chosen this way should be confirmed on fresh data; and whether its improvement is larger than sampling noise is a question for the model-comparison page. ## The Lorenz curve and the Gini index The lift chart shows separation decile by decile. The **Lorenz curve** shows it as one continuous curve: 1. sort the policies from the **lowest** to the **highest** prediction, 2. walk along the sorted list and plot the **share of total exposure** covered so far (x-axis) against the **share of total claim cost** it contains (y-axis). A model that can't separate risks (the Null model) gives the diagonal: the first 30% of exposure carries 30% of the claim cost. A model that separates well puts little claim cost into its low-risk policies, so its curve sags below the diagonal. The **oracle** sorts by the actual outcome, the best ranking possible. ::: {#cell-fig-lorenz .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = plot_lorenz(y, {m: p[m] for m in models}, w) ax.figure.set_size_inches(5.5, 5.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Lorenz curves on the test set, policies sorted from lowest to highest prediction. The dashed curve sorts by the actual outcome.](lift-lorenz_files/figure-html/fig-lorenz-output-1.png){#fig-lorenz width=554 height=547} ::: ::: The GBM's lowest-risk half of the exposure carries only 32% of the claim cost. The **Gini index** condenses the curve into one number: twice the area between the diagonal and the curve, $$ \text{Gini} = 1 - 2 \int_0^1 L(x)\,dx, $$ where $L(x)$ is the share of claim cost in the lowest-predicted share $x$ of the exposure. It is 0 for the Null model and grows the better the model ranks the policies. The two models score 0\.293 (GLM) and 0\.294 (GBM), a relative difference of 0\.6%. On D² the GBM was 6% ahead, and its top-to-bottom lift was much larger. The Gini weighs the whole ranking, while the lift ratio looks only at the two extreme deciles, each resting on a few hundred claims. A single decile ratio is a much noisier summary than the Gini. The oracle's Gini of 0\.984 is not a realistic target: 95% of the exposure had no claim at all, and only hindsight can put those policies first. Some authors report a **normalized Gini** (Gini ÷ oracle Gini), but the oracle mostly reflects how many policies happened to have no claims, so it adds little here. ::: {.callout-note} ## Relation to the classification Gini The [ROC page](../binary/roc-auc.qmd) defined Gini = 2·AUC − 1 for a binary target. For a 0/1 outcome with equal weights, the Lorenz Gini equals $(1 - \pi)(2 \cdot \text{AUC} - 1)$, where $\pi$ is the share of positives (the tests in `tests/` check this). The factor $1 - \pi$ is the oracle's Gini: dividing by it gives the normalized Gini, which equals 2·AUC − 1. Both measure how well the model ranks. The Lorenz version extends the idea to outcomes that aren't 0/1, such as claim cost, and to weighted observations. ::: ### What the Gini can't see The Gini depends **only on the ranking**. Any transformation that keeps the order of the predictions leaves it unchanged, however wrong the predictions become: ::: {#tbl-gini-blind .cell tbl-cap='Three versions of the GBM with identical rankings. \'Squared\' is GBM², rescaled to the same average, so its overall level is right but its spread is far too wide.' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} squared = p["GBM"] ** 2 * np.average(p["GBM"], weights=w) / np.average(p["GBM"] ** 2, weights=w) variants = {"GBM": p["GBM"], "2 × GBM": 2 * p["GBM"], "GBM squared": squared} pd.DataFrame({ name: { "Gini": gini_index(y, s, w), "D²": deviance_metrics(y, s, p["Null"], w, TWEEDIE_POWER)["D²"], "bias (EUR)": regression_metrics(y, s, w)["bias"], } for name, s in variants.items() }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
GBM 2 × GBM GBM squared
Gini 0.2944 0.2944 0.2944
D² 0.0134 -0.0050 -0.0186
bias (EUR) -3.6890 138.9580 -3.6890
``` ::: ::: Doubling every prediction, or squaring them, keeps the Gini exactly the same. D² drops below 0 (worse than predicting the average for everyone), and a lift chart would show the gap at once. So: - **Never use the Gini alone.** Pair it with a lift chart or a calibration check, and with the deviance. - **Don't compare Ginis across portfolios or years.** Like AUC, the Gini depends on how heterogeneous the population is: a portfolio with more varied risks gives a higher Gini for an equally good model. - **Small differences are noise.** The GLM and GBM differ by 0\.002, far less than the test-set variability of a Gini on data this noisy. Testing such differences is the subject of the model-comparison page. ## Which tool for which question | Tool | Answers | Watch out for | |---|---|---| | Lift chart | Does cost rise with the prediction, and does the prediction match per segment? | noisy deciles: read the intervals | | Double lift chart | Where two models disagree, which is right? | rebalance both models to the same level first | | Lorenz curve / Gini | How well does the model rank risks, in one number? | blind to calibration and level; not comparable across portfolios | | Deviance / D² | How good are the individual predictions, ranking and level together? | small values are normal; hard to interpret alone | The tools complement each other: the Gini and the lift spread measure **ranking**, the agreement in the lift chart measures **calibration by segment**, the double lift chart **compares** two candidate models, and the deviance checks both ranking and level at once. ## Takeaways - With noisy outcomes, judge a pricing model on **groups**: deciles of equal exposure average away the noise that dominates individual-level metrics. - A **lift chart** should rise monotonically, be steep, and have predictions that run through the actual points. Here the GLM overpredicts its top decile by 23%. - A **double lift chart** compares two models where they disagree. Here each model finds mispricing in the other, and a simple **blend** beats both. - The **Gini index** summarizes the Lorenz curve: 0\.293 (GLM) against 0\.294 (GBM). It measures ranking only, so a badly miscalibrated model can have the same Gini as a good one.
